A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on preserving LLM security during instruction fine-tuning, retaining the classifier-based module analysis and robust-subset search. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier, module-perturbation, safety, usability, and mathematical-task experiments, including detailed appendix results.

after.justification: v2 reports original safety/task comparisons, feature-space analyses, parameter-update measurements, and instruction-modeling ablations in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: v1's ML-LR applies different learning rates to robust and remaining modules throughout tuning. v2's SWAT instead warms up only robust modules, adding instruction modeling with loss over instructions and responses, then trains all targeted LoRA parameters. The classifier-guided search remains a foundation, but the training procedure and objective substantially change (Section 3.3).

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Alpaca-based general instruction tuning and learning privately defined mathematical operators. v2 replaces these tasks with UltraInteract logical reasoning and GSM8K word problems, using Alpaca as supplementary training data, and adds training contaminated with malicious examples. Security coverage replaces Just-Eval with CatQA and removes GCG, while retaining Advbench and four other jailbreak methods.

E2.justification: v1 compares ML-LR principally with BASE and standard IFT. v2's Llama2-7B comparisons add evaluated defense baselines LoRAsafe, IFTsafe, Resta, and Resta integrated with DARE, labeled Restad (Tables 2–3). These are substantive additions to the comparator set.

E3.justification: ASR changes from GPT-judged harmfulness exceeding 1 to rule-based detection of security expressions, and the harmfulness judge changes from GPT-4-1106-preview to GPT-4o. v2 also revises training budgets and sample counts, adds 4- or 16-epoch warm-up stages before IFT, and changes the model suite, dropping Vicuna and 13B evaluations while adding Qwen2-7B. The default LoRA targets, rank 8, and alpha 16 remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds classifier transfer across base/tuned/SWAT representations, intermediate warm-up performance, parameter-update analysis, and an instruction-modeling ablation (Tables 1, 4, 7; Figure 5). v1's control for insufficient data fitting and all-module LoRA experiment disappear. Layer-depth verification remains, but its models change and the middle-layer condition is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Averages across attacks and deterministic perturbations do not establish uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v1's Alpaca and private-mathematics results are largely replaced by SWAT results on new tasks and scenarios. For example, v2 Table 2 reports UltraInteract ASR of 61.18% for IFT versus 27.82% for SWAT, with task accuracy of 66.00% versus 66.80%. Table 5 additionally reports complete language failure for one combined-defense configuration. These are newly reported outcomes under changed conditions, not demonstrated performance gains over v1's ML-LR.

T1.justification: v2 adds Equation 3, defining a contrast between SWAT and standard-IFT parameter-update L2 norms. The classifier and perturbation-accuracy equations remain substantively equivalent. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from differentiated learning rates specifically for benign IFT to SWAT for both benign and attack-contaminated IFT. v2 adds security-feature-space drift as a central explanatory claim and explicitly claims compatibility with existing pre-training and post-training defenses.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations involving early-layer drift amplification and allocation of low-level versus task-relevant learning across module subsets. It qualifies module-type sensitivity as model-dependent, including different behavior in Qwen2. Its new limitations section acknowledges coarse analysis granularity, security loss during warm-up, residual risks, and drift being only one possible cause.

D1.justification: The technical recipes are substantially revised: v2 documents model-specific warm-up durations, instruction-token training, attack-data additions, and defense implementation details such as IFTsafe's 1,000 security samples. v1's dual-learning-rate recipes and synthetic-mathematics construction appendix disappear. Search pseudocode remains, but v2 does not retain comparable explicit checkpoint-selection guidance.

R1.justification: v1 positions itself as pioneering mitigation for benign IFT. v2 reorganizes the landscape into pre-training, in-training, and post-training defenses, discussing Bianchi, Hsu, Bhardwaj, and Wei et al. (2024b) as relevant alternatives. Added feature-drift and instruction-modeling references support a substantially revised rationale and novelty positioning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively rewritten around SWAT and feature-space drift. Experimental preparation and results are reorganized into a consolidated main-experiment section, the scenario organization changes, and dedicated limitations and ethical-considerations sections are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. The framework diagram is redrawn, main radar-chart presentations give way to expanded safety/task tables, and the robust-subset map moves from the appendix into the main text. New parameter-update plots and ablation tables accompany substantial changes to existing figure and table structures.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1: comparison chiefly against ordinary IFT. Evaluations against established defenses make safety/task tradeoffs substantially more assessable, while new mechanism checks and the instruction-modeling ablation strengthen support for the revised method. The gains are tempered by removal of earlier fitting and all-module controls and an overbroad compatibility claim: Table 5 reports complete language failure for one combination. Overall, the stronger comparative evidence represents a substantial quality improvement.
